text.p: The Bangladesh Nationalist Party called on opposition parties on Saturday to join a united campaign against Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her alleged "secret deals" with big neighbour India.

BNP chief Begum Khaleda Zia, a former prime minister and Hasina's arch foe, issued the appeal at a "solidarity conference" in Dhaka attended by leaders of several right-wing parties including the orthodox Jamaat-e-Islami and the radical Jatiya Ganatantrik Party.
The meeting marked a new line-up against Hasina's nine-month-old Awami League government and behind the "India-bashing" which Khaleda has made her main theme.
But analysts said the anti-Delhi campaign has not yet won wide support among Bangladeshis longing for political stability and economic development.
Khaleda accused Hasina of tilting too much towards India -- which backed her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman when he led Bangladesh's 1971 war for independence from Pakistan.
"The Independence and sovereignty of our motherland are threatened because of a conspiracy by the government. Let us unite to face it," she told the meeting.
Khaleda accused Hasina of being "shamelessly pro-Indian" and vowed to resist "secret deals" between Dhaka and New Delhi.
"They have recently signed deals to allow India a land transit and corridor through Bangladesh," the BNP leader said. "This will jeopardise our national security."
"They (the government) have surrendered our economic freedom and our foreign policy at the hands of another country. Time has come for all of us to foil this conspiracy," Khaleda said.
Hasina last week offered to have talks with her rival to defuse political tension.
"She has made secret deals, keeping the parliament and nation in dark. Now she is calling for talks. It's a mockery," Khaleda said on Saturday.
Khaleda also criticised Hasina's handling of the economy, saying major economic indicators were giving worrying signals.
"Revenue shortfall had forced a huge deficit financing in recent months, raising inflation rate as high as 10 percent," she said.
"Now the government is running after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for a $600 million loan as foreign exchange reserves have tumbled to $1.6 billion," Khaleda added.
Government statistics, however, gave the current inflation rate at around four percent and the reserves at about $1.8 billion.
